chapter_theme: A Vidyadhara sky-car lands to bring joy over the birth in Tivittan's house, a Vidyadhara messenger tells how the sun-named lord's wife dreamt of a gem and bore the boy Amitatejas, Tivittan rewards him, and his own son grows, goes to teachers at five, and a younger daughter is born and named amid kin and joy.

1723.reading: After word of the joy has been sent to the Vidyadhara world as well and the dark-hued lord has given his leave, a red-gold sky-car comes down out of the cloudy heavens.
1723.nuance: The sense of lines 1-2 (what is sent, and what the dark-hued lord grants) is not fixed; ஓகை is taken as 'joy', the news of the birth in chapter 74.
1723.event: A red-gold flying car descends from the sky to the lord's city.

1724.reading: Seeing a gem-bright flying car come down and reach the city, the spear-bearing lord tells his people it is the lords' own visit and bids them bring what is due to the guests.
1724.nuance: Line 3 (பணிவரை கொணர்மினீர்) is hard; 'bring what is fit for service' is the reading taken.
1724.event: Tivittan sees the sky-car land and orders his men to bring the welcome.

1725.reading: The Vidyadhara women, bright of body, come down with their chamberlains from the car that enters the rain-cloud, and reach the king's lodging in the walled city.
1725.event: The Vidyadhara women and their attendants alight and reach the palace.

1726.reading: At the cry 'Let it flourish!' the women pour fragrant ghee over the long golden crown, and a great laugh of love rises loud as the roaring sea.
1726.nuance: Whose crown or head is anointed is not said; given the birth in chapter 74 it may be the child's, but the verse names only the king (புரவலன்) and the women.
1726.event: The women pour ghee at the lord's word and the hall breaks into joyful laughter.

1727.reading: After the ghee-anointed women are sent to the women's palace and the seated company settles, one man bows to the queen's lord and begins to tell him a tale.
1727.nuance: 'பாவை கோயில்' is taken as the women's quarters, and 'யாங்கிருந்த' as the company's sitting; who 'we' are is not stated.
1727.event: A Vidyadhara messenger bows to Tivittan and begins his report.

1728.reading: The messenger says that our lord, whose name is the shining sun, dwells in delight with the garlanded daughter of the mountain-king whose hair is like a dark cloud.
1728.nuance: 'எறிகதிர்ப் பெயரன்' is taken as Arkakirti (the sun-named), the Vidyadhara prince of the earlier chapters; the wife is called சோதிமாலை, which may be a name or an epithet.
1728.event: The messenger names the Vidyadhara lord of the sun's name and his wife, daughter of the mountain king.

1729.reading: One night while the king's wife sleeps the moon rises in the sky with its rays and opens the blossoms of the wide heavens.
1729.nuance: The rising of the moon over her sleep is the frame for her dream of the next verse, as the moon's entry is the frame of the dream in chapter 74.
1729.event: The moon rises over the sleeping queen.

1730.reading: After a cool gem has come to her in a dream, her breasts swell and she takes the form of a bright goddess like a gold figure.
1730.event: After her dream of the gem the queen shows the signs of pregnancy.

1731.reading: Climbing the gem-bright sky-car and seeing the wish-tree groves, the doe-eyed woman lets her pregnancy craving be satisfied.
1731.nuance: 'வயா' is the craving of pregnancy; in the verse the satisfaction of the craving is told as a flight over the wish-tree groves.
1731.event: The queen rides the sky-car through the heavenly groves and her craving is satisfied.

1732.reading: After she has become like a gold figure, a youth appears with a body so bright that even the moon in the bent sky would be shamed by it.
1732.event: The queen's son is born, radiant as a young moon.

1733.reading: The child, with a red lily's petals, a coral mouth, eyes like fragrant flowers and a face like the inside of a lotus, is like a babe of gold in the flower.

1734.reading: As the boy appears, gem lamps burn in the sky, flower rain falls with bees, conches sound like the sea's waves, and light spreads in every direction.
1734.event: Heavenly signs accompany the child's birth: lamps, a rain of flowers, conches and light.

1735.reading: Sovereign kings of boundless strength had their old white umbrellas wilt as he rose with boundless strength, and they gave him a name that says that very might: Amitatejas.
1735.nuance: The name 'அளப்பருந் திறலினன் அமித தேசன்' is repeated word for word in each line to make the meaning, 'of unmeasurable might', plain; who gives it is left to 'they'.
1735.event: The boy is named Amitatejas ('boundless might').

1736.reading: The speaker ends his report: the dark-cloud-hued uncle, to let the lord's beauty be drunk by the eyes, said 'tell the world's master and come', and so he has come with ghee; such is the matter.
1736.nuance: Who is meant by மாமனார் (the child's uncle) and by 'the master of the world' is not clear; the text says only that a message of 'come' was sent. Line 1 carries a repaired pulli.
1736.event: The messenger finishes his report and states that he came bringing ghee.

1737.reading: On hearing him the lord of the discus gives him treasure shining in the vault, joins him to royal wealth, and the messenger goes happily to his own world.
1737.event: Tivittan rewards the messenger with treasure and he returns to the Vidyadhara world.

1738.reading: Tivittan's son, the child of the foe-less lord of the golden discus, grows with a beauty that makes onlookers glad, guarded by women with hair full of bees.
1738.nuance: After the news of Amitatejas the verse returns to Tivittan's own son (called the lord's child, not by name here); the earlier chapter names him Vijayan.
1738.event: Tivittan's son grows up in the care of his nurses.

1739.reading: Guarded by many shining gods and blessed by the lotus lady, he grows like the cool-rayed sun in the sky, a lord of cool light over the earth.
1739.nuance: The 'many gods' who guard him are the poem's own picture of a fortunate birth; the verse does not link them to any school.
1739.event: The child grows under the care of gods and the goddess of the lotus.

1740.reading: With golden-corded anklets ringing, gem strings shining at his waist and golden bells on his feet, he crawls about the courtyards of the women who wear gold-corded jewels.
1740.event: The boy crawls about the women's courtyards in his jewels.

1741.reading: Shown the golden lotuses of the pond and called by women of gentle form, he is glad, and his ear-rings flash like lightning as he creeps through the pollen-laden gardens.
1741.event: The boy plays among the garden pools while women call him.

1742.reading: The ones who see him see the wealth of eyes, the earth's wealth grows with his joy each day, and like the red sun of the heavens he plays and tires, pulling the little golden wheel.
1742.nuance: Three kinds of wealth (of the eyes, of the earth, of the sky) are used for the child, as one fortune seen from three sides.
1742.event: The boy plays with a golden wheel-toy until he is tired.

1743.reading: At the age of five the boy is brought to teachers rich in unfailing learning, so that the lord of the bright discus unites him with them.
1743.nuance: 'காதலி நாவின் மகளாக' (line 2) is hard; it may mean the boy is joined to learning as to a loved one's own daughter. The reading here takes only the sure part: teachers and the boy at five.
1743.event: Tivittan hands his five-year-old son to learned teachers.

1744.reading: The queen of the guardian lord bears a girl, younger than the boy, whom all the world calls the god of love's wealth and who rises praised in every direction like the fire-offering's wealth.
1744.nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard: 'காமச் செல்வன்' may name the boy, or praise the girl, who is the one 'ஒளியாள்' who is praised.
1744.event: Tivittan's queen gives birth to a daughter younger than her son.

1745.reading: The assembled kin, the Vidyadhara kinsfolk among them, name her in keeping with victory, are sent back to the Vidyadhara ranks, and the dark-hued lord sinks happily in a sea of love and joy.
1745.nuance: The name given, 'பெயரிட்டு' with 'கொன்றிய வாறு', is not given in the verse and is hard to construe; 'in keeping with victory' is a guess.
1745.event: The kin gather and give a name; the Vidyadhara guests leave; Tivittan is full of joy.

1746.reading: So the boy grows, the great queen is full of joy, and the girl, whom they obtained by worshipping the gods like fortune itself that the people worship, has a name of lightning for her body's light.
1746.nuance: 'மின்னின் பெயராளும்' ends the verse with her name as the name of lightning; the name is not spelled out and a later chapter's heroine may be this girl or another.
1746.event: The boy and the girl grow up; the queen rejoices.

links.note: 1706 has the moon enter the queen's mouth as the sign of Tivittan's son; 1730 has a gem come to the Vidyadhara wife in a dream and swell her breasts.
links.teaches: The poem uses the same dream of a bright thing entering the mother for two houses, so the Vidyadhara child's birth is told as a parallel of Tivittan's own.

links.note: 1712 shows Tivittan's son born in saffron-bright radiance; 1732 shows the Vidyadhara boy born with a face to shame the moon.
links.teaches: The two births are drawn with one image, the lit young body, which lets the later chapters set the two boys side by side as equals.

links.note: 1735 names the boy Amitatejas for his boundless might; 1791 has the prince Amitatejas enter the swayamvara hall so bright that other kings are dimmed.
links.teaches: The name given at birth is made good at the swayamvara, so the boy's later outshining of kings is shown as the sign promised at his birth.

links.note: 1721 has Tivittan show jewels and gold to his guests and invite them to take them; 1737 has him give a share of his treasure to the Vidyadhara messenger.
links.teaches: The giving at the son's birth and at the nephew's news both follow the same open-handedness, so Tivittan is drawn as a king whose joy is shown by giving.

links.note: 1743 has Tivittan give his five-year-old son to teachers 'rich in unfailing learning'; Kural 67 says a father's good to his son is to put him first in the assembly.
links.teaches: The Kural names the goal of a father's care, the seat in the assembly; the epic shows the first step toward it, early schooling in the hands of learned men.

gains.a: The prince's schooling gains a stated purpose, that the father's good lies in the son's standing among the learned, not his wealth.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete first step, a royal father handing a child of five to teachers, which the couplet does not name.

links.note: 1743 calls the teachers 'rich in unfailing learning' (பொய்யாக் கல்விச் செல்வர்); Kural 400 says learning is the one wealth that does not perish.
links.teaches: The epic uses the language of wealth for learning, which Kural 400 claims for it alone, but gives it to men who serve a king whose other wealth is shown at length.

gains.a: The teachers gain the Kural's ground for the title 'rich', that their wealth is the one that does not fail.
gains.b: The couplet gains a court where learning and the other wealth stand together, a test of whether learning is the only wealth.

links.note: 1745 has the father sink in a sea of joy at the naming and the gathering of kin; Kural 69 says a mother is gladder to hear her son called worthy than at his birth.
links.teaches: The epic's joy comes at the naming and the kin's praise, while the Kural puts the greater joy later, in the son's worth, so the verse's delight is the first joy, not the last.

gains.a: The father's delight gains a measure, that it is the joy of the birth and the Kural counts a greater one still to come.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene of a father's joy at the naming, a joy of the birth that it sets as the lower mark.

links.note: 1738 has the child grow in the guard of women who tend him; Naladiyar 20 says Death takes even the newborn while the mother wails.
links.teaches: The poem's guarded growth is the thing the quatrain says cannot be guaranteed, so the child's safety is read against death's stealth.

gains.a: The guarded child gains the quatrain's reminder that guard does not keep death off, which the poem does not say.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a child as well cared for as can be, the strongest case for its warning.

links.note: 1730 gives the dream of a gem as the sign that the child is coming; Tirumanthiram 453 says the Lord, at the moment of the joining, fixes the span and the earthly life of the child.
links.teaches: The epic reads the conception from omens and the mother's body, while the Tirumanthiram says the life was fixed by the Lord at the joining, so a sign is read against a cause.

gains.a: The gem-dream gains a view in which the child's fate is already fixed, before the sign comes.
gains.b: The verse of Tirumular gains a conception told as a royal dream, a case where signs are read as promises.

links.note: 1746 closes with the girl whose name is that of lightning growing up; 1750 shows the young women's ball-play at the swayamvara chapter's start.
links.teaches: The girl born here grows into the maiden of the later chapters, so the birth is the root of the swayamvara story.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark-hued lord with the discus, host of the Vidyadhara guests
the men whom Tivittan orders to bring the welcome
the Vidyadhara women who alight with chamberlains and pour the ghee
the Vidyadhara man who bows to Tivittan and reports the birth
the mountain-king's daughter, wife of the sun-named Vidyadhara lord, who conceives and bears Amitatejas
the Vidyadhara prince born in the messenger's story; id as in chapter 77
Tivittan's own son, who grows, crawls and is sent to school; id as in chapter 74
Tivittan's queen, who bears a daughter; id as in chapter 74
the many kin who gather and name the girl

source_issues: 1736 line 1 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed by the build.
1738 line 3 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed by the build.
1743-1746 are in a different metre and their last lines are hard to construe; the sense of 1743 line 2, 1744 lines 1-2 and 1745 line 2 is not fixed.
The identity of the girl born in 1744-1746 is not stated; chapters 76-78 may call her Sayambavai.
